title: Passions spurned
hook: the prince explains why pleasures don't satisfy: fire isn't quenched by fuel (Buddhacarita 11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bimbisara's visit, and a generous offer of half a kingdom. Your line: half a kingdom.

Throw a log on a fire and ask it whether it's had enough. It hasn't. It's bigger now, and hungrier. That's the picture at the center of the prince's answer to King Bimbisara, who has just offered him half a kingdom and a sensible plan for enjoying life in its season. The prince doesn't brush the king off. He takes the offer seriously enough to give a whole canto of reasons, and the fire is where he begins.
screen: `A LOG ON THE FIRE.` → `BIGGER, AND HUNGRIER.` → `A WHOLE CANTO OF REASONS.`

segments.voice: First, the respect. Before any argument, the prince honors the king's kindness: it's no surprise, he says in paraphrase, that a man of good family would offer friendship like this, and he's grateful. Second, the fire. Pleasures don't satisfy. A fire isn't quenched by fuel, and the sea isn't filled by the rivers that run into it. Feed a desire and you don't end it; you make it larger. Someone who gets what they wanted wants more; someone who gets more fears losing it. Third, the pictures. The poem piles them up. Pleasures are like a dog gnawing a dry bone, never fed by it. Like a scrap of meat that birds fight over. Like a torch of straw carried into the wind, which burns the hand that holds it. Like a dream that's gone when you wake. Like borrowed jewelry that has to be given back. Each says the same thing from a different side: what we reach for to soothe the burning keeps the burning going. Fourth, the parting. He tells the king he isn't running from enemies or from hardship. He's going after freedom, and he can't be turned aside by a kingdom any more than by threats. And the poem ends gently. Bimbisara joins his palms, wishes him success, and asks one favor: when you've found what you're seeking, come back and show it to me. The prince promises. He turns down the passions, not the king. He refuses half a kingdom and keeps a friend.
screen: `HE HONORS THE KING'S KINDNESS.` · `FIRE ISN'T QUENCHED BY FUEL.` · `A BONE, A TORCH, A DREAM.` · `COME BACK AND SHOW ME.` · then, large: `FUEL DOESN'T QUENCH FIRE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one want that keeps coming back however often you feed it, one more thing to buy, a craving for praise, or sugar, or being right, and picture feeding it: does it go quiet, or flare up? No scolding; just watch the fire. Then, for the rest of the sit, add nothing to it, and see what it does without fuel.
Passions spurned. The prince turns down Bimbisara's kingdom, explaining that pleasures feed desire the way fuel feeds fire, and parts from the king as a friend. Today's word.
Your line: fuel doesn't quench fire. The poem ends with a promise to come back. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use fire as a picture of craving, and in the Pali discourses the Buddha's Fire Sermon describes the senses as burning; in some Buddhist meditation practices people watch a craving rise and fall without acting on it.

chat.says: Why turn down half a kingdom? Couldn't he enjoy it and still seek freedom?
options: He said pleasures grow when fed, like fire with fuel, so they never satisfy.
He said the king's offer insulted him, and he refused to be bought.
He said he'd enjoy the kingdom later, once he'd found what he sought.
chat.meaning: A fire isn't quenched by fuel: feeding a desire only makes it larger, so pleasures can't give the freedom he seeks.

Bimbisara.meaning: the king of Magadha who offered half his kingdom
